title: Turkey
subtitle: 1980–today · The Generals, Özal's Opening, the Kurdish War, the Justice and Development Decades, and the Presidential System

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The generals and Evren, Özal, the coalition decade, Gül and the Erdoğan years, and the presidential system

entries.label: Kenan Evren
entries.hint: General Kenan Evren, chief of the general staff, led the National Security Council that seized power on 12 September 1980 and was head of state under the regime, and was confirmed as president for seven years by the referendum of 7 November 1982, which approved the new constitution. He left office in November 1989 at the end of his term. In 2014 he was convicted of crimes against the state for the coup and sentenced to life, and he died in 2015 before the appeal was settled.
entries.note: NSC Communiqué no. 1 (12 September 1980); Law no. 2709 (1982); verdict of the Ankara court (18 June 2014); William Hale, Turkish Politics and the Military (1994).

entries.label: Turgut Özal as president
entries.hint: Özal, prime minister since 1983, was elected president by the assembly on 31 October 1989 and was the first civilian president in nearly thirty years to hold real influence on policy, involving himself in the Kurdish question and the Gulf War of 1991. He died suddenly in office on 17 April 1993.
entries.note: TBMM records (31 October 1989); Erik Zürcher, Turkey: A Modern History (1993/2004).

entries.label: Süleyman Demirel
entries.hint: Demirel, the veteran leader of the centre-right who had been prime minister seven times, was elected the ninth president on 16 May 1993 and served the single seven-year term, during which the military pushed the Welfare-led government out on 28 February 1997. His term ended in May 2000.
entries.note: TBMM records (16 May 1993); Zürcher 2004.

entries.label: Ahmet Necdet Sezer
entries.hint: Sezer, a judge and the president of the Constitutional Court, was elected on 5 May 2000 as a candidate agreed between the parties. He used his veto often against the AKP governments after 2002 and was seen as the defender of the secular state.
entries.note: TBMM records (5 May 2000); Zürcher 2004.

entries.label: Abdullah Gül
entries.hint: Abdullah Gül, an AKP founder and foreign minister, was elected president by the assembly on 28 August 2007 after a presidential election crisis in which the army posted a warning and the Constitutional Court annulled the first vote. His candidacy was the first in which the president's wife wore a headscarf at the palace. He left office in August 2014 and was the last president elected by the assembly.
entries.note: TBMM records (28 August 2007); Constitutional Court decision (1 May 2007); Zürcher 2004.

entries.label: Recep Tayyip Erdoğan as president
entries.hint: Erdoğan was elected on 10 August 2014 in the first direct presidential election with 51.8 per cent, re-elected in June 2018 under the new executive presidency, and again in the second round of 28 May 2023 with 52.2 per cent. Under the system of 2017 he is both head of state and head of government. His tenure continues as of 2026.
entries.note: Supreme Election Council results (10 August 2014; 24 June 2018; 28 May 2023).

entries.label: The military regime and the Ulusu government
entries.hint: The National Security Council dissolved parliament, banned the parties, arrested the party leaders and appointed Admiral Bülend Ulusu prime minister of a cabinet of officers and technocrats, with Turgut Özal as deputy prime minister for the economy until 1982. It governed by decree with martial law until the elections of November 1983.
entries.note: NSC Law no. 2356 (1980); Hale 1994.

entries.label: Turgut Özal's governments
entries.hint: The Motherland Party under Turgut Özal won the election of 6 November 1983 with 45 per cent of the vote against the generals' favoured candidate and governed alone for six years. It liberalised the economy, opened the country to exports and imports, and applied for membership of the EEC in 1987. The 1983 election also began the return to civilian rule.
entries.note: Election results (6 November 1983); Zürcher 2004.

entries.label: The coalition decade
entries.hint: From 1989 to 2002 no party won a majority after the end of Özal's, and coalitions of Demirel and Çiller (DYP), Mesut Yılmaz (ANAP), Erbakan (RP, 1996–1997) and Ecevit (DSP, 1999–2002) followed one another, with short lives, in years of the Kurdish war, the military's 'postmodern coup' of 1997 and a banking sector in crisis. Tansu Çiller became Turkey's first woman prime minister in 1993.
entries.note: TBMM records; election results (1991, 1995, 1999); Zürcher 2004.

entries.label: The AKP governments under Gül and Erdoğan
entries.hint: The Justice and Development Party, founded in 2001 by Erdoğan and others from the Welfare tradition, won 34 per cent of the vote and two-thirds of seats in November 2002 and then won the elections of 2007, 2011 and, after a hung parliament in June 2015, November 2015. Abdullah Gül (2002–2003), Erdoğan (2003–2014), Ahmet Davutoğlu (2014–2016) and Binali Yıldırım (2016–2018) were prime ministers until the post was abolished.
entries.note: Supreme Election Council results (2002, 2007, 2011, June and November 2015); Zürcher 2004; Metin Heper (ed.), The Justice and Development Party (2013).

entries.label: The presidential system
entries.hint: After the referendum of 16 April 2017 and the elections of 24 June 2018, the post of prime minister was abolished and executive power passed to the president, assisted by vice presidents (Fuat Oktay, then Cevdet Yılmaz from 2023) and appointed ministers. The AKP governs with the nationalist MHP in the People's Alliance. This arrangement continues as of 2026.
entries.note: Law no. 6771 (2017); Supreme Election Council (2018, 2023).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The coup of 1980, the PKK war and its end, the Sivas and Ankara bombings, Gezi, the coup attempt of 2016 and the cross-border operations

entries.label: The coup of 12 September 1980
entries.hint: At 4 a.m. on 12 September 1980 the armed forces under General Evren took power, in the third military intervention of the Republic after months in which party deadlock had left the assembly unable to elect a president and street violence was killing some twenty people a day. About 650,000 people were detained in the following years, hundreds died in custody, and 50 were executed. Parties, trade unions and associations were closed, and the universities placed under a Higher Education Council.
entries.note: NSC Communiqué no. 1; Hale 1994; Zürcher 2004; Turkish Human Rights Association.

entries.label: The PKK's war
entries.hint: The Kurdistan Workers' Party, founded in 1978 under Abdullah Öcalan, began its armed campaign on 15 August 1984 with attacks at Eruh and Şemdinli. In four decades of war the fighting killed well over 40,000, soldiers, guerrillas and civilians; thousands of villages in the southeast were evacuated by the army; and a state of emergency applied in the region from 1987 to 2002. The PKK demands have included autonomy and independence and then cultural rights; the Turkish state and many governments consider it a terrorist organisation. In 2025 it announced its dissolution (see the peace process).
entries.note: PKK founding congress (1978); Turkish General Staff; Human Rights Foundation of Turkey; Hamit Bozarslan, Kurdish Nationalism in Turkey; Zürcher 2004.

entries.label: The Sivas massacre
entries.hint: On 2 July 1993 a crowd, after the Friday prayers, set on fire the Madımak Hotel in Sivas, where Alevi writers, musicians and intellectuals had gathered for a cultural festival; 33 guests and two hotel staff died. Police and soldiers did not stop the crowd for hours. Trials in the 1990s and 2000s convicted some of the participants, and the case file was closed by the statute of limitations in 2012 for those still at large.
entries.note: Ankara State Security Court verdicts (1997); Court of Cassation; Massicard, The Alevis in Turkey and Europe (2013).

entries.label: Susurluk and the 'deep state'
entries.hint: A car accident at Susurluk on 3 November 1996 killed a police chief, a fugitive ultranationalist wanted for murder and a woman companion, and left a Kurdish tribal chief and True Path Party deputy, Sedat Bucak, injured, and exposed ties between the security forces, organised crime and politicians in the war against the PKK. The parliamentary and prime-ministerial investigation reports were published, but few were punished.
entries.note: Prime Ministry Inspection Board (Kutlu Savaş) report (January 1998); TBMM Susurluk Commission report (1997).

entries.label: The 'postmodern coup' of 28 February 1997
entries.hint: At a meeting of 28 February 1997 the National Security Council, dominated by the generals, presented the coalition government of Necmettin Erbakan with a list of measures against 'reactionary' political Islam: closing the religious schools' middle sections, restricting the headscarf and the orders. Erbakan resigned on 18 June, and the Constitutional Court banned the Welfare Party in January 1998. Without a coup in the formal sense, the army had forced out an elected government.
entries.note: NSC resolution of 28 February 1997; Constitutional Court decision (16 January 1998); ECtHR, Refah Partisi v. Turkey (2003).

entries.label: Öcalan's capture
entries.hint: Öcalan, who had fled from Syria in October 1998 after Turkish threats, was seized by Turkish agents in Nairobi on 15 February 1999 and tried on the prison island of İmralı; he was sentenced to death in June 1999 and the sentence commuted to life when the death penalty was abolished in 2002. The PKK declared a ceasefire in September 1999. He remains the movement's leader from prison.
entries.note: Ankara State Security Court verdict (29 June 1999); Law no. 4771 (2002); ECtHR, Öcalan v. Turkey (2005).

entries.label: The murder of Hrant Dink
entries.hint: Hrant Dink, the editor of the Armenian weekly Agos, who had been convicted under Article 301 of insulting Turkishness, was shot dead outside his newspaper in Istanbul on 19 January 2007 by a 17-year-old nationalist. Some 100,000 people attended his funeral. The European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2010 that Turkey had failed to protect him, and later trials, including a verdict of 2021, convicted former police and gendarmerie officials; the question of wider responsibility remains open.
entries.note: ECtHR, Dink v. Turkey (14 September 2010); Istanbul Assize Court verdicts (2012, 2021).

entries.label: The settlement process and its collapse
entries.hint: In 2012–2013 the government and Öcalan negotiated, with the Kurdish party BDP and later the HDP as intermediaries, a 'resolution process' that brought a ceasefire in March 2013, the withdrawal of PKK fighters and a statement at Dolmabahçe in February 2015. It broke down in July 2015 after the Suruç bombing and the killing of two policemen, and in 2015–2016 urban fighting and curfews in Cizre, Sur and other towns left hundreds dead and large districts destroyed.
entries.note: Newroz declaration (21 March 2013); Dolmabahçe statement (28 February 2015); UN OHCHR report on southeast Turkey (March 2017).

entries.label: The Gezi protests
entries.hint: A sit-in against the plan to redevelop Gezi Park in Taksim, attacked by police with tear gas on 31 May 2013, grew into the largest demonstrations in the Republic's history, with protests in some 80 provinces. At least eight protesters and a police officer died and thousands were hurt. The government called it a plot, the demonstrators a defence of public space and freedom; Osman Kavala was later imprisoned for it and the European Court of Human Rights found his detention unlawful in 2019.
entries.note: Interior Ministry statements (2013); Turkish Medical Association report; ECtHR, Kavala v. Turkey (10 December 2019).

entries.label: The bombings of Suruç and Ankara
entries.hint: A suicide bomber killed 33 young socialist volunteers bound for Kobani at Suruç on 20 July 2015, and two suicide bombers killed more than a hundred people at a peace rally at Ankara railway station on 10 October 2015, the deadliest attacks in the Republic's history. The attacks were attributed to the Islamic State. They came during the collapse of the settlement process and the election campaign.
entries.note: Prosecutor's indictments (Ankara, 2016–2017); Interior Ministry statements.

entries.label: The attempted coup of 15 July 2016
entries.hint: On the night of 15 July 2016 a faction of the armed forces seized the Bosphorus bridges, bombed the parliament and the presidential complex and attempted to take Erdoğan; citizens and loyal forces and police defeated it by morning. About 250 people were killed, apart from the plotters, and some 2,000 were wounded. The government blames the movement of the preacher Fethullah Gülen, once an ally, which denies it; the Gülen network was designated a terrorist organisation (FETÖ), and its role is the subject of many trials.
entries.note: Interior Ministry and General Staff statements; TBMM Investigation Commission report (2017); Turkish courts' verdicts (2017–2021).

entries.label: The purge
entries.hint: Under the state of emergency from 20 July 2016 to 19 July 2018, decrees-law dismissed some 125,000 civil servants, judges, teachers and officers, closed thousands of associations, media outlets and schools, and tens of thousands were detained or tried for links with the Gülen movement or other groups. An inquiry commission set up in 2017 reinstated some. Critics at the Council of Europe and UN called the measures disproportionate; the government defended them as necessary to protect the state.
entries.note: Emergency decrees (KHK) nos. 667–701; Inquiry Commission on State of Emergency Measures (2017); Venice Commission opinion (March 2017).

entries.label: The operations in Syria and Iraq
entries.hint: Turkish forces and allied Syrian opposition groups entered northern Syria in August 2016 (Euphrates Shield), in January–March 2018 took Afrin (Olive Branch) and in October 2019 a strip east of the Euphrates (Peace Spring), each against the Syrian Kurdish YPG which Turkey considers an extension of the PKK. Ankara's partners and some governments criticised the operations and the human cost; Turkey cited its security. Operations against the PKK in northern Iraq continued.
entries.note: Turkish General Staff statements; UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria reports; Zürcher 2004 (background).

entries.label: The peace process of 2025–2026
entries.hint: On 27 February 2025 Öcalan called on the PKK to lay down its arms and dissolve; the organisation announced its dissolution in May, a first group destroyed weapons at a ceremony in Iraqi Kurdistan in July, a parliamentary commission was set up in August, and its report was approved on 18 February 2026. A law framing the reintegration of members was passed by the assembly on 10 August 2026 with the votes of the AKP, MHP and DEM Party. As of 2026 its implementation is under way and the outcome is open.
entries.note: Öcalan's call (27 February 2025); PKK statement (12 May 2025); commission report (18 February 2026); TBMM vote (10 August 2026).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The constitution of 1982, the emergency regimes, the EU reforms, the referendums of 2007 to 2017 and the Istanbul Convention

entries.label: The constitution of 1982
entries.hint: The constitution drafted by the National Security Council's appointed assembly was approved on 7 November 1982 by 91.4 per cent in a referendum in which campaigning against it was prohibited, and it provided at the same time for Evren's presidency. It strengthened the executive and the National Security Council, restricted trade unions, associations and the press, and an election law of 1983 set a 10 per cent national threshold for parliamentary representation. The constitution has been amended many times since.
entries.note: Constitution no. 2709 (7 November 1982); Zürcher 2004.

entries.label: The state of emergency in the southeast
entries.hint: Under decree-law no. 285 of July 1987 an emergency region governorship was set up for several southeastern provinces, with powers to evacuate villages, ban publications and assign officials, and it was extended in four-month periods until it was lifted in November 2002. The legal state of exception became the normal form of government in the region.
entries.note: Decree-law no. 285 (10 July 1987); Parliamentary Research Commission on evacuated villages (1998).

entries.label: The EU reform packages
entries.hint: In the run-up to the accession talks, parliaments passed constitutional amendments in 2001 and 2004 and a series of 'harmonisation packages' which abolished the death penalty in peacetime (2002) and in all cases (2004), allowed broadcasting and education in minority languages, curbed the National Security Council, and removed military judges from the State Security Courts. The reforms were later partly reversed in practice.

entries.label: The presidential crisis and the referendum of 2007
entries.hint: When the AKP nominated Abdullah Gül for the presidency in April 2007, the General Staff published a warning on its website on 27 April, secular demonstrations were held, and the Constitutional Court annulled the vote on a quorum ruling. The government called early elections, which it won in July with about 47 per cent, and a referendum on 21 October 2007 established the direct election of the president by 69 per cent.
entries.note: General Staff statement (27 April 2007); Constitutional Court decision (1 May 2007); referendum results (21 October 2007).

entries.label: The Ergenekon and Sledgehammer trials
entries.hint: From 2007 prosecutors indicted hundreds of retired and serving officers, journalists, academics and politicians on charges of conspiring to overthrow the AKP government, in the Ergenekon and Sledgehammer cases; verdicts of 2012–2013 sentenced many, among them a former chief of the general staff. The evidence was later widely found to include forged digital material, convictions were overturned from 2014, and the proceedings are now widely seen, including by the government that had backed them, as having been manipulated by the Gülen network.
entries.note: Istanbul Assize Courts verdicts (2012, 2013); Constitutional Court decisions (2014); Court of Cassation (2016, 2019).

entries.label: The AKP closure case
entries.hint: A case brought by the chief prosecutor in March 2008 asked the Constitutional Court to ban the AKP and bar Erdoğan and 70 others from politics for anti-secular activity. On 30 July 2008 six of the eleven judges voted to close it, one short of the seven needed; the court instead cut the party's state funding by half.
entries.note: Constitutional Court decision E.2008/1 (30 July 2008).

entries.label: The referendums of 2010 and 2017
entries.hint: The constitutional referendum of 12 September 2010, approved by 58 per cent, changed the composition of the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Council of Judges and Prosecutors and ended the legal immunity of the 1980 coup leaders. The referendum of 16 April 2017, approved by 51.4 per cent amid a state of emergency and with disputed counting, replaced the parliamentary system with an executive presidency from 2018.
entries.note: Laws nos. 5982 (2010), 6771 (2017); Supreme Election Council results; Venice Commission opinion (March 2017).

entries.label: The state of emergency of 2016–2018
entries.hint: After the coup attempt, parliament declared a three-month state of emergency on 20 July 2016, extended seven times until 19 July 2018, in which more than thirty decrees with the force of law were issued, which suspended some constitutional safeguards, allowed dismissals by decree and restricted detention rights. Turkey derogated from the European Convention on Human Rights during it.
entries.note: Council of Ministers decision (20 July 2016); Council of Europe notification of derogation (21 July 2016).

entries.label: The withdrawal from the Istanbul Convention
entries.hint: Turkey was the first country to ratify, in 2012, the Council of Europe's Convention on preventing violence against women signed at Istanbul in 2011, and the first to leave: a presidential decree published on 20 March 2021 withdrew it, with effect from 1 July. The government said the convention had been 'hijacked' by groups undermining family values; women's organisations protested, and the Council of State upheld the decree in 2021.
entries.note: Presidential decree no. 3718 (20 March 2021); Council of State decision (July 2021); Council of Europe Treaty no. 210.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The headscarf, Hagia Sophia, the Alevi opening and the Welfare and AKP parties

entries.label: The headscarf question
entries.hint: After the coup the headscarf was barred in universities and public offices by regulations and by a Constitutional Court decision of 1989, a ban upheld by the European Court of Human Rights in the Leyla Şahin case (2005). It was eased in universities in 2010–2013, abolished for public servants by regulation in October 2013 and in high schools in 2014, as a major symbol of the conflict between secularists and the religious.
entries.note: Constitutional Court decisions of 1989 and 2008; ECtHR, Leyla Şahin v. Turkey (10 November 2005); regulation of 8 October 2013.

entries.label: The Directorate of Religious Affairs and the imam-hatip schools
entries.hint: The 1982 constitution made religious instruction compulsory in schools, and the Diyanet's budget and staff grew to well over 100,000 employees, among the largest public bodies. The imam-hatip schools, originally meant for training clergy, expanded to a large share of secondary schooling after the 1980s; the 1997 measures restricted them, and the AKP governments removed the restrictions.
entries.note: Constitution (1982), art. 24; Diyanet budget laws; Zürcher 2004.

entries.label: From the Welfare Party to the AKP
entries.hint: Erbakan's Welfare Party (founded 1983) won the most votes in the 1995 election and led a coalition in 1996–1997, after winning Istanbul and Ankara in 1994 under Erdoğan and Melih Gökçek. After the party's closure, its younger leaders founded the AKP in August 2001 as a conservative-democratic party that accepted the secular system and the EU goal, and won the election of 2002.
entries.note: Election results (1994 local, 1995 general, 2002); Constitutional Court decision (16 January 1998); Heper (ed.) 2013.

entries.label: The Alevi opening
entries.hint: After the Sivas massacre of 1993 Alevi organisations and federations multiplied and demanded the legal recognition of cemevis, the end of compulsory Sunni religious lessons and equal status for Alevism. A government 'opening' of 2009–2010 held workshops but did not grant legal status to cemevis; the European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2007 and 2014 that the compulsory lessons violated the Convention, and in 2014 that denying cemevis the status of places of worship was discriminatory.
entries.note: ECtHR, Hasan and Eylem Zengin v. Turkey (2007); Cumhuriyetçi Eğitim ve Kültür Merkezi Vakfı v. Turkey (2014); Mansur Yalçın v. Turkey (2014).

entries.label: Hagia Sophia returned to worship
entries.hint: On 10 July 2020 the Council of State annulled the cabinet decree of 1934 which made Hagia Sophia a museum, and a presidential decree the same day transferred it to the Directorate of Religious Affairs as a mosque; the first Friday prayer was held on 24 July. Supporters called it a restoration of the legal status of a waqf building; UNESCO, the Orthodox churches and other governments regretted the change.
entries.note: Council of State decision (10 July 2020); presidential decree no. 2729 (10 July 2020).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Yol and the Palme d'Or, Orhan Pamuk's Nobel, Eurovision and the television drama

entries.label: Yol and the Palme d'Or
entries.hint: Yılmaz Güney's film Yol (The Way), written in prison and directed by Şerif Gören to his instructions, shared the Palme d'Or at Cannes in May 1982 with Costa-Gavras's Missing; it follows five prisoners on leave in a Turkey under martial law. It was banned in Turkey until 1999. In 2014 Nuri Bilge Ceylan's Winter Sleep won the Palme d'Or alone.
entries.note: Cannes Festival, 1982 and 2014 awards; Zürcher 2004.

entries.label: Eurovision and the television drama
entries.hint: Sertab Erener won the Eurovision Song Contest for Turkey in Riga in May 2003. In the same decade Turkish television serials became one of the country's main exports, with series such as Muhteşem Yüzyıl (2011–2014) and Gümüş sold across the Middle East, Balkans and Latin America, and Turkey became one of the world's largest drama exporters.
entries.note: Eurovision 2003 results; TRT and Turkish export statistics.

entries.label: Orhan Pamuk and the Nobel Prize
entries.hint: Orhan Pamuk, the novelist of Istanbul, author of The White Castle, My Name Is Red and Snow, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature on 12 October 2006, the first Turkish citizen to win it. He had been prosecuted in 2005 for remarks to a Swiss newspaper about the killing of Armenians and Kurds in Turkey; the case was dropped.
entries.note: Nobel Prize in Literature 2006; Istanbul Şişli court (2005–2006).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The Turkish-Islamic synthesis, strategic depth, and the public debate on the Armenian and Kurdish questions

entries.label: The Turkish-Islamic synthesis in the schools
entries.hint: The military regime adopted the 'Turkish-Islamic synthesis' of the Intellectuals' Hearth as its ideology to counter the left: compulsory religious instruction, a revised national history curriculum and a Higher Education Council (YÖK, 1981) to control the universities. It shaped the generation educated in the 1980s.
entries.note: Law no. 2547 (Higher Education, 1981); Constitution art. 24; Aydınlar Ocağı publications; Zürcher 2004.

entries.label: Strategic depth
entries.hint: Ahmet Davutoğlu's book Stratejik Derinlik (2001) argued that Turkey should exploit its position and Ottoman and Islamic heritage to become a central power in its region rather than a Western outpost, and as advisor and foreign minister from 2003 to 2014 he guided a policy of 'zero problems with neighbours' which was often called neo-Ottomanism. The Arab uprisings put the policy to the test.
entries.note: Ahmet Davutoğlu, Stratejik Derinlik (2001); Zürcher 2004; Kalın and others.

entries.label: The debate on the Armenian question
entries.hint: In September 2005 a conference of Turkish historians at Istanbul's Bilgi University discussed the Ottoman Armenians despite a court order and attacks by the justice minister and nationalists. Article 301 of the 2005 penal code, which punished 'denigrating Turkishness', was used against Pamuk, Dink and others and was amended in 2008. In December 2008 several hundred intellectuals signed an 'I apologise' campaign, which was denounced by the government and nationalists.
entries.note: Penal Code art. 301 (2005; amended 2008); Bilgi University conference (24–25 September 2005); 'Özür diliyorum' petition (December 2008).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The decisions of January 1980, the export model, the crises of 1994, 2001 and 2018, and the inflation years

entries.label: The export model of the 1980s
entries.hint: After the decisions of 24 January 1980, the military regime and Özal's governments devalued the lira, cut subsidies, gave export credits and tax rebates, and removed import quotas; exports rose from 2.9 billion dollars in 1980 to 11.7 billion in 1989, and a larger share was manufactures. Workers' real wages fell. In 1989 the capital account was opened.
entries.note: Decisions of 24 January 1980; Decree no. 32 (1989); Şevket Pamuk, Uneven Centuries (2018); Zürcher 2004.

entries.label: The Southeastern Anatolia Project
entries.hint: The GAP, planned since the 1970s and developed from 1989 under its own administration, aimed to build 22 dams and 19 power plants on the Euphrates and Tigris and irrigate 1.7 million hectares in the southeast; the Atatürk Dam was completed in 1992 and the Şanlıurfa tunnels in 1995. The project raised cotton and electricity output and was also contested by Syria and Iraq over river waters, and for its flooding of heritage sites such as Hasankeyf (2020).
entries.note: GAP Regional Development Administration; Law-decree no. 388 (1989); Hasankeyf flooding (2019–2020).

entries.label: The crises of 1994 and 2001
entries.hint: Public deficits and short-term borrowing led to a currency crisis in April 1994 (the 5 April decisions) and, with a weak banking sector, to the crisis of November 2000 and February 2001, when the lira was floated, the economy shrank by about 6 per cent and many banks were taken over by the state. The IMF programme and Kemal Derviş's reforms restored stability.
entries.note: Decisions of 5 April 1994; Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency (2000); IMF stand-by agreement (December 1999 and 2002); Pamuk 2018.

entries.label: The growth years of the 2000s
entries.hint: With the IMF programme, a strong banking sector, falling inflation to single digits, large capital inflows and the EU anchor, the economy grew at about 5 per cent a year from 2002 to 2012 and the per capita income tripled in dollar terms. The growth depended on foreign borrowing and construction.
entries.note: TÜİK national accounts; Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey; Pamuk 2018.

entries.label: The currency crisis of 2018 and the inflation years
entries.hint: The lira fell by roughly a third against the dollar in 2018 amid a diplomatic dispute with the United States and concern about the Central Bank's independence, and again in 2021 after interest-rate cuts against the advice of economists. Official annual inflation peaked at 85.5 per cent in October 2022, which independent researchers said understated it; a return to orthodox policy under Mehmet Şimşek from June 2023 raised rates sharply.
entries.note: TÜİK consumer price index; Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey; ENAG; Pamuk 2018.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The Atatürk Dam, Marmaray, the third bridge and the airport, and the defence industry

entries.label: Marmaray and the bridges
entries.hint: The Fatih Sultan Mehmet Bridge opened in 1988 as Istanbul's second Bosphorus crossing; the Marmaray tunnel carrying commuter rail under the strait opened on 29 October 2013 and the Yavuz Sultan Selim Bridge, the third bridge, in August 2016, with the Eurasia road tunnel (2016) and Istanbul Airport (2018) following. They tied the two sides of the city.
entries.note: Marmaray opening (29 October 2013); Yavuz Sultan Selim Bridge opening (26 August 2016); Istanbul Airport opening (29 October 2018).

entries.label: The armed drone and the defence industry
entries.hint: From an embargo on arms after 1975 and the 1990s, the state's SSB agency, Aselsan, TAI and private firms such as Baykar built a national defence industry. The Bayraktar TB2 armed drone was used in Syria, Libya, Nagorno-Karabakh and Ukraine, and Turkey became a significant arms exporter by the 2020s. The Togg national electric car was introduced in 2023.
entries.note: SSB (Presidency of Defence Industries) reports; SIPRI arms transfers data; Togg launch (29 October 2022; deliveries 2023).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The customs union and the EU talks, the Annan plan, S-400 and CAATSA, Syria and the refugees

entries.label: Northern Cyprus and the Annan plan
entries.hint: The Turkish Cypriot assembly declared the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus on 15 November 1983, recognised only by Turkey; the UN Security Council termed the declaration legally invalid. In the referendum of 24 April 2004 on the UN's Annan plan, about 65 per cent of Turkish Cypriots voted yes and 76 per cent of Greek Cypriots no, and the island entered the EU on 1 May as a divided island. As of 2026 the division continues.
entries.note: UN Security Council res. 541 (1983) and 550 (1984); Annan plan referendum results (24 April 2004).

entries.label: The customs union and the EU talks
entries.hint: Turkey applied for membership of the European Community in 1987, entered a customs union with the EU on 1 January 1996, was declared a candidate at the Helsinki summit of December 1999 and opened accession negotiations on 3 October 2005. The talks stalled from 2006 over Cyprus and other issues, and have been frozen in practice since 2018.
entries.note: Association Council decision 1/95 (1995); Helsinki European Council conclusions (December 1999); European Council (17 December 2004); Council conclusions (June 2018).

entries.label: The Syrian war and the refugees
entries.hint: Turkey, which supported the Syrian opposition from 2011, took in the largest number of Syrian refugees in the world, about 3.7 million at the peak in 2021, under a 'temporary protection' regime, and in March 2016 agreed with the EU a statement on migration for funds and visa talks. After the fall of the Assad government in December 2024 hundreds of thousands returned; official counts in 2025 still gave some two to two and a half million remaining.
entries.note: Law no. 6458 (2013) and Temporary Protection Regulation (2014); EU–Turkey Statement (18 March 2016); Presidency of Migration Management statistics.

entries.label: The S-400 and the CAATSA sanctions
entries.hint: Turkey bought the Russian S-400 air-defence system in 2017, took delivery in July 2019 and tested it in October 2020, after which the United States removed it from the F-35 programme (July 2019) and imposed sanctions on the defence procurement agency in December 2020 under the CAATSA law. NATO allies said the system was incompatible with allied defences.
entries.note: US Department of State statement (14 December 2020); White House statement (17 July 2019).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The earthquakes of 1999 and 2023, the Syrian refugees and the growth of the cities

entries.label: The growth of the cities
entries.hint: The census of 1980 counted 44.7 million people; the register-based count for 2023 gave about 85 million. In the same period the urban share rose from 44 per cent to around 77 per cent, Istanbul grew from 4.7 million to 15.5 million and the birth rate fell from about 4 children per woman to about 1.6, below the replacement rate.
entries.note: TÜİK census 1980; Address-Based Population Registration System (2023); TÜİK birth statistics.

entries.label: The Kurdish displacement and the migration to the west
entries.hint: During the war in the southeast the army and the village guards evacuated or destroyed villages and hamlets, in a number which official bodies put at around 3,000 settlements and others higher, displacing, by the estimates of a 2006 Hacettepe University study, between 950,000 and 1.2 million people to the towns of the region and the cities of the west. The Law on Compensation of Losses of 2004 allowed claims.
entries.note: Hacettepe University Institute of Population Studies, Türkiye Göç ve Yerinden Olmuş Nüfus Araştırması (2006); Law no. 5233 (2004).

entries.label: The Izmit earthquake
entries.hint: A magnitude 7.6 earthquake on the North Anatolian Fault at 3:02 a.m. on 17 August 1999 struck the industrial heart of the Marmara region, killing about 17,500 people by official figures (some estimates are higher) and leaving hundreds of thousands homeless. The failure of the state's response and of construction controls led to a building code reform and an earthquake tax.
entries.note: Kandilli Observatory; Prime Ministry Crisis Management Centre; compulsory earthquake insurance (DASK, 2000).

entries.label: The Kahramanmaraş earthquakes
entries.hint: Two earthquakes of magnitudes 7.8 and 7.5, hours apart, on 6 February 2023 along the East Anatolian Fault destroyed large parts of 11 provinces including Kahramanmaraş, Hatay, Adıyaman and Gaziantep, and killed more than 50,000 people in Turkey (the official figure is 53,537) and some 6,000 in Syria. Hundreds of thousands of buildings were destroyed or damaged, and the response and the building amnesties of earlier governments were widely criticised.
entries.note: AFAD (Disaster and Emergency Management Presidency) reports; Presidency of Strategy and Budget damage assessment (2023).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The women's movement and the Istanbul Convention, Kurdish language, the diaspora and the generation of Gezi

entries.label: The women's movement and violence against women
entries.hint: Women's organisations grew after 1980 and won reforms to the civil code (2001, equal rights in the family) and the penal code (2004, removal of 'honour' and 'chastity' provisions); a 2012 law on protection from violence followed the Istanbul Convention. Femicide figures kept by civil society groups, such as 'We Will Stop Femicide', run to several hundred a year and are higher than the official counts, which the government does not publish in full.
entries.note: Civil Code no. 4721 (2001); Penal Code no. 5237 (2004); Law no. 6284 (2012); We Will Stop Femicide Platform annual reports.

entries.label: The Armenian community and the memory of 1915
entries.hint: The Armenian community of Turkey, about 50,000–60,000 people mostly in Istanbul, keeps its churches, schools and press, including Agos, and since the murder of Hrant Dink has been at the centre of a debate on 1915. In April 2014 Erdoğan, as prime minister, offered condolences to the grandchildren of those who died in 1915 for the first time; the state rejects the word genocide. Armenia's border with Turkey is closed.
entries.note: Prime Ministry statement (23 April 2014); Zürcher 2004; Armenian Patriarchate of Istanbul.

entries.label: The migrants in Europe
entries.hint: After the recruitment stop of 1973 the Turkish population of Germany grew through family reunion and births, to up to two million Turkish citizens in the 1990s and some 2.8 million people of Turkish origin by the 2010s, and communities were established in Austria, the Netherlands, France and Belgium. The 1999 German citizenship reform gave the German-born children German nationality by birth.
entries.note: German Federal Statistical Office (Mikrozensus); German Nationality Act reform (1 January 2000).

entries.label: The Kurdish language
entries.hint: Law no. 2932 of 1983 forbade the use of Kurdish in publications and public speech; it was repealed in April 1991, but radio and television broadcasting in Kurdish was permitted only from 2002 and the state channel TRT 6 opened in January 2009. Private Kurdish courses were permitted in 2003, election campaigning in Kurdish in 2010 and elective lessons in state schools from 2012.
entries.note: Law no. 2932 (1983), repealed by Law no. 3713 (1991); Law no. 4771 (2002); TRT Şeş (1 January 2009); 4+4+4 education law (2012).

entries.label: The generation of Gezi
entries.hint: The protests of 2013 brought a young generation without a party into the squares, many of them born after 1990. They used social networks to organise, and in the following years the state tightened its control of the internet and social media, with laws of 2014, 2020 and 2022, and blocked access to Twitter, Wikipedia (2017–2020) and other sites.
entries.note: Law no. 5651 as amended (2014, 2020); Constitutional Court decision on Wikipedia (26 December 2019); Law no. 7418 (2022).
